question: A study group debates matrix multiplication. Which claim is accurate?
options: Any two matrices can be multiplied in either order.
Matrix products always have the same shape as the inputs.
Matrix multiplication is associative but generally not commutative.
gold_answer: Matrix multiplication is associative but generally not commutative.
notes: Team-authored original item on matrix multiplication. Passages are team-authored derivations recorded under sciclaim-appx-A. Requires independent annotation and adjudication before any gate result is reported.

positions.answer: Any two matrices can be multiplied in either order.

evidence.text: Grouping of consecutive products can change without altering the result, as the triple-product expansion shows.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states grouping does not alter the result, which entails the claim.

evidence.text: Multiplication distributes over addition, satisfying the distributive expansion.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage affirms distributivity, which refutes the claim.

claims.text: Matrices solve every computational problem fastest.

evidence.text: Running times were compared for matrix and non-matrix approaches on one task.

claims.verdict_rationale: One comparison cannot show universal superiority, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.

positions.answer: Matrix multiplication is associative but generally not commutative.

claims.text: The identity matrix leaves any compatible matrix unchanged.

evidence.text: Multiplying by the identity reproduces each entry exactly, acting as the multiplicative unit.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage describes exact reproduction, which entails the claim.

claims.text: AB always equals BA for square matrices.

evidence.text: Rotations and scalings in different orders give different results, providing counterexamples to commutativity.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage gives counterexamples to commutativity, which refutes the claim.

claims.text: All linear systems have unique solutions.

evidence.text: Solution counts were classified across a set of example systems.

claims.verdict_rationale: Classifying examples cannot show all systems are unique, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.

claims.text: The product of an m-by-n and an n-by-p matrix is m-by-p.

evidence.text: Each entry combines a row of the first with a column of the second, giving m rows and p columns.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage derives the m-by-p shape, which entails the claim.

claims.text: The product of two non-zero matrices is always non-zero.

evidence.text: Zero divisors exist among matrices, so non-zero factors can multiply to the zero matrix.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states non-zero factors can yield zero, which refutes the claim.

evidence.text: Determinant values were computed for matrices of several dimensions.

claims.verdict_rationale: Computing values cannot show determinants measure size, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.
